subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which term describes the lifelong process by which people learn the norms and values of their society?
questions.explain: Socialisation is the process of learning the culture (norms and values) of a society.

questions.q: A newborn learning to speak and use a knife and fork from their family is an example of which stage of socialisation?
questions.explain: Primary socialisation happens first, mainly within the family, learning basic skills and norms.

questions.q: A teacher, peer group or the media shaping a teenager's behaviour are agents of which type of socialisation?
questions.explain: Secondary socialisation occurs later through agents beyond the family such as school, peers, media and religion.

questions.q: In sociology, 'culture' is best defined as...
options: The whole way of life of a society, including its norms, values and beliefs
The wealth owned by a society
questions.explain: Culture is the shared way of life of a group: its norms, values, beliefs, customs and language.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches the definitions?
options: Norms are laws; values are customs
Norms and values mean the same thing
Norms = general beliefs about right and wrong; Values = specific rules of behaviour
Norms = specific rules of expected behaviour; Values = general beliefs about what is important/desirable
questions.explain: Norms are specific expected behaviours; values are broader beliefs about what is good and worthwhile.

questions.q: Queuing politely at a shop counter is an example of a...
questions.explain: Queuing is an informal expected behaviour in a situation, i.e. a norm.

questions.q: An 'ascribed status' is one that is...
options: Given at birth or fixed, such as being born into a royal family
The same as a social role
questions.explain: Ascribed status is fixed/given (e.g. by birth), unlike achieved status which is earned.

questions.q: Becoming a doctor after years of study is an example of...
questions.explain: Achieved status is gained through a person's own efforts and choices.

questions.q: Feral child cases (e.g. children raised without human contact) are used by sociologists mainly to argue that...
options: Human behaviour is largely learned through socialisation, not just biology
questions.explain: Feral children lack normal human behaviour, supporting the 'nurture' view that behaviour is socially learned.

questions.q: Functionalism views society as...
options: A set of individual meanings and labels
A structure of interconnected parts working together for stability and consensus
questions.explain: Functionalists (e.g. Durkheim, Parsons) see society as a stable system based on shared values and consensus.

questions.q: Which sociologist is a key functionalist associated with 'social solidarity' and 'value consensus'?
questions.explain: Durkheim, a founding functionalist, emphasised social solidarity and shared values holding society together.

questions.q: Marxism argues that society is shaped mainly by...
options: Conflict between the ruling class (bourgeoisie) and working class (proletariat)
questions.explain: Marxists see society as divided by class conflict between the bourgeoisie (owners) and proletariat (workers).

questions.q: In Marxist theory, the group that owns the means of production is called the...
questions.explain: The bourgeoisie own the means of production; the proletariat sell their labour.

questions.q: Feminist sociologists argue that society is best described as...
questions.explain: Feminists argue society is patriarchal, with institutions benefiting men and disadvantaging women.

questions.q: Which type of feminism sees patriarchy as the root cause of women's oppression?
questions.explain: Radical feminists see patriarchy itself as the fundamental cause of women's oppression.

questions.q: Interactionism is a perspective that focuses on...
options: Small-scale, everyday interactions and the meanings people attach to them
questions.explain: Interactionism is a micro perspective studying how meanings and labels are created through interaction.

questions.q: The idea that a label given to a person can shape how they see themselves and behave is known as the...
questions.explain: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when a label leads a person to act in line with it.

questions.q: A 'positive sanction' is best described as...
options: A punishment for breaking a norm
A reward for conforming to norms
questions.explain: Positive sanctions reward conformity; negative sanctions punish deviance.

questions.q: A police force and courts are examples of which type of social control?
questions.explain: Formal social control is exercised by official agencies with written rules, such as the police and courts.

questions.q: A person's sense of who they are, shaped by factors like gender, ethnicity, class and nationality, is their...
questions.explain: Identity is a person's sense of self, shaped by social factors and socialisation.
